topic: WeWork: from a 47 billion dollar valuation to bankruptcy
title: WeWork Was Worth $47 Billion. It Was Just Renting Offices
alt_titles: The Office Company That Thought It Was a Tech Giant
pinned_comment: Was Adam Neumann a genius salesman or just lucky with investors? What do you think?
sources_to_check: Losses of about 1.9 billion dollars in 2018 on revenue of about 1.8 billion
The 5.9 million dollar payment for the "We" trademark, later returned
SPAC listing in 2021 and bankruptcy filing in November 2023
description:
In 2019, investors valued WeWork at 47 billion dollars, more than many famous tech companies. Its business? Renting offices and subletting them. Months later, the IPO collapsed, the founder was out, and in 2023 WeWork filed for bankruptcy.

This is the story of Adam Neumann, the charismatic founder who convinced the world's biggest tech investor that a real estate company was the future, and of the IPO document that revealed the truth.

• Two founders and a coworking idea
• Masayoshi Son and billions from SoftBank
• Elevating the world's consciousness
• The IPO filing that changed everything
• Bankruptcy and a billion dollar exit for the founder

segments.text: In January 2019, one startup was valued at around 47 billion dollars. More than many airlines, more than famous tech brands. Its founder said the company would elevate the world's consciousness. Its business? Renting office space, decorating it nicely, and renting it out again. Less than a year later, the company had cancelled its stock market debut, its founder was gone, and billions of dollars in value had evaporated. In 2023, it filed for bankruptcy. This is the story of WeWork.

It starts in New York with two founders. Adam Neumann, a tall, charismatic Israeli entrepreneur who had tried businesses like baby clothes with knee pads, and Miguel McKelvey, an architect. In 2008, after the financial crisis, many offices in New York were empty and many people were starting small businesses. The two men had a simple idea: take an empty building, divide it into small, beautiful shared offices, and rent desks to freelancers and startups by the month.

In 2010, they opened the first WeWork in Manhattan. The offices had glass walls, cool furniture, free coffee and even free beer. There were events, parties and a sense of community. For young entrepreneurs, working at WeWork felt much better than working alone at home or in a boring old office. Buildings filled up quickly. And Neumann realized that he was not selling desks. He was selling a lifestyle.

And Neumann was an extraordinary salesman. He did not describe WeWork as a real estate company. He described it as a technology company, a community company, a company that would change how the world lives and works. That difference matters enormously. Real estate companies are valued as slow, stable businesses. Technology companies can be valued at huge numbers because investors expect explosive growth. Neumann wanted the tech valuation.

Then came the man who would change everything: Masayoshi Son, the Japanese billionaire who runs SoftBank. Son had made a fortune investing early in Alibaba, and he had just created a gigantic investment fund, the Vision Fund, with around 100 billion dollars. According to reports, Son visited WeWork's offices with Neumann for only a few minutes and quickly decided to invest billions. Son reportedly told Neumann to be crazier and to think ten times bigger.

And Neumann did. With SoftBank's money, WeWork expanded at an incredible speed, opening locations in dozens of countries, sometimes several per week. It launched a school, called WeGrow. It launched apartments, called WeLive. It bought a wave pool company and invested in all sorts of strange businesses. It became the biggest private office tenant in New York. Growth was everything, and profit could wait. If you like these stories about billion dollar mistakes, subscribe, because there are many more to come.

Neumann's own lifestyle became legendary. Private jets, huge houses, tequila shots with employees, surfing trips. But some of his business decisions were even stranger. He bought buildings with his own money and then rented them to WeWork, his own company. And when the company changed its name to The We Company, it paid Neumann around 5.9 million dollars for the rights to the word we, because he had registered the trademark himself. After public criticism, he gave the money back.

Inside the company, the culture felt more like a movement than a job. There were weekly Monday parties called Thank God It's Monday. Every summer, thousands of employees traveled to a camp in the English countryside for a festival called Summer Camp, with famous bands and plenty of alcohol. Employees worked long hours, but many truly believed they were part of something historic. Neumann spoke about becoming the first trillionaire and even about living forever. The energy was contagious. And it made it very hard for anyone inside to ask the boring question: how does this company actually make a profit?

But the biggest problem was the business model itself. WeWork signed leases with building owners for ten or fifteen years. Then it rented desks to customers who could leave after one month. So WeWork had huge long term obligations, and very short term income. In good times, that works. But if a crisis arrives and customers leave, WeWork still has to pay rent for years. It is not a tech company. It is a very risky real estate company.

In August 2019, WeWork published the document required before going public, called an S one. And for the first time, the world could see the numbers. In 2018, WeWork had lost around 1.9 billion dollars on revenue of around 1.8 billion. It had tens of billions of dollars in future lease obligations. The document talked about elevating the world's consciousness. And it used a strange metric called community adjusted EBITDA, which basically removed many normal costs to make the numbers look better.

The reaction was brutal. Analysts, journalists and investors read the document and started laughing, or panicking. The conflicts of interest, the losses, the founder's control over the company, everything looked terrible. The expected valuation started dropping, from 47 billion to 20 billion, and then even lower. In September 2019, under enormous pressure, Adam Neumann stepped down as CEO. A few days later, WeWork cancelled its IPO.

SoftBank had to rescue the company, investing even more money. And here is the part that made people furious: Neumann left with a package reported to be worth more than a billion dollars, including money for his shares and a consulting fee. Meanwhile, thousands of WeWork employees lost their jobs, and many of them had stock options that were now worth very little. The founder who created the mess left richer than ever.

Then, in 2020, the pandemic hit. Offices around the world emptied overnight. For a company with long, expensive leases and customers who could leave after a month, it was a nightmare. WeWork still managed to go public in 2021, through a special type of company called a SPAC, at a value of around 9 billion dollars. That is less than a fifth of its famous 47 billion dollar valuation. And the losses continued.

In November 2023, WeWork filed for bankruptcy. It closed many locations and renegotiated leases with landlords. The company still exists, much smaller, but its shares were practically wiped out. SoftBank lost billions of dollars on the investment. Masayoshi Son later admitted publicly that his investment in WeWork was a mistake and said he had been foolish.

And Adam Neumann? In 2022, he started a new real estate company called Flow, focused on apartments. And one of the most famous venture capital firms in Silicon Valley, Andreessen Horowitz, invested around 350 million dollars in it, before it had even really started operating. For many people, that was the most surprising twist of the whole story.

So what is the lesson of WeWork? Changing the name of a business does not change what the business is. WeWork said it was a tech company, but it made money like a landlord and took risks like a gambler. Investors wanted to believe in a story more than they wanted to read the numbers. And when somebody finally read the numbers, 47 billion dollars turned out to be mostly an idea.
Now tell me in the comments: do you think Adam Neumann was a genius salesman, or just lucky to meet the right investor at the right time? And would you give him money for his next company?

segments.text: In 2019, WeWork was valued at 47 billion dollars. Its business? Renting offices for years and subletting desks month by month. The founder called it a tech company that would elevate the world's consciousness. He even charged his own company 5.9 million dollars for the word we. Then WeWork published its numbers: around 1.9 billion dollars lost in one year. The IPO was cancelled, and in 2023 WeWork went bankrupt. The full story is on the channel.
